What every engagement delivers

Four answers a capital decision depends on.

Each traces to the site’s own records, a cited benchmark or a documented assumption, so your lender can reproduce it.

About the platform
  1. 01

    Verified member count

    Members reconciled to billing records and tested for duplicates, dormancy and failed payments. What remains is active, unique and collectible.

  2. 02

    Normalized earnings

    Add-backs, one-time items, rent and maintenance capital tested line by line, so EBITDA reflects what the site earns under new ownership.

  3. 03

    A price the data supports

    Value built from verified earnings and a market multiple, with every deal adjustment and the gap to the asking price shown.

  4. 04

    A priced operating plan

    Membership, pricing, labor and throughput levers, each sized in dollars, risk-adjusted and sequenced.

The platform

Proprietary analytics, built by operators.

Every Wise Wash Partners engagement runs on a proprietary analytics platform developed from years of running car washes. It reads a site’s own point-of-sale, membership and billing data, and traces every figure to an input, a cited benchmark or a documented override.

Controls

Same inputs, same result.

Traceable

Every figure traces to an input, a benchmark with a cited source, or an override recorded in an audit register.

Reproducible

A client’s lender can rerun the file and reach the same answer.

Source data only

Three components, one verified file

From raw exports to a supportable value.

Membership verification

What the membership base is worth. Membership is the largest single driver of an express wash’s value and the hardest to see in a report. The platform reads the roster, the wash log, the billing history and the point-of-sale audit log, and tests every row.

It identifies

  • Duplicate accounts and plates with no active vehicle
  • Dormant accounts still counted as members
  • Paused accounts and churn not yet surfaced
  • Promotional spikes and price step-up overhang
  • Conversion and back-office adjustments

It produces

  • Verified member count and collectible recurring revenue
  • Lifetime value by plan and commitment length, using survival analysis
  • A bridge from the reported base to the verified base
  • A verification workbook a lender or accountant can open and test
Membership retention, illustrative
Share of members remaining, by month since joining
Retention reaches 49% at month 24 against a 53% regional benchmark. A representative site, not a client engagement.

Operating benchmarking

Where the next dollar of earnings comes from. The platform scores a site or portfolio against published regional benchmarks, identifies each area of concern and prices every lever: the earnings it is worth, the ramp and the payback. Every input and assumption can be overridden, and the change flows through the whole plan.

It prices

  • Dunning, churn and membership conversion
  • Pricing, plan structure and retail ticket
  • Labor and each cost line
  • Water reclaim, capacity and throughput
  • Marketing

It produces

  • A benchmark scorecard for the site or portfolio
  • Areas of concern ranked by the earnings at stake
  • A sequenced plan with anticipated results, ramp and payback for each lever

Full underwrite

From raw exports to a supportable value, in one file. Sixteen modules carry a site from raw point-of-sale exports to a supportable value, a financeable capital structure and a written record of every assumption behind them.

It covers

  • Membership verification at row level
  • Trade area capture within three and five miles, with the permit pipeline weighted
  • P&L normalization, with add-backs credited by category
  • Current and future value on sourced multiples
  • Capital structure and debt service across the full term
  • Scenarios, Monte Carlo simulation, a risk register and an override register

It produces

  • An underwriting report and workbook
  • A supportable value and a downside case
  • A lender package organized for a credit process
  • Side-by-side comparison and portfolio roll-up across sites

Roster forensics

The seller's export carried 4,508 rows: 3,919 active, 187 paused and 402 already cancelled. The active rows are the starting population; the schedule below is what survives inspection.

DeductionFlaggedWeightMembers removedMRR effectWhy it is deducted
Duplicate accounts106.0100.0%105.4-$3,033Same plate, card or contact appearing more than once. Only the excess above one is deducted.
Phantom plates63.0100.0%63.0-$1,813Active subscription with no vehicle or plate identifier attached.
Non-transactional members248.040.0%99.1-$2,852No wash inside the dormancy window — elevated cancel probability, not yet cancelled.
Card-at-risk accounts118.055.0%64.7-$1,862Declined or expired card still carried as active; net of expected dunning recovery.
Paused / zombie accounts187.00.0%0.0$0187 paused rows sit OUTSIDE the active base and its MRR, so nothing is deducted for them here. They matter if the seller's headline count includes them — check the reconciliation — and as suppressed churn.
Members carrying multiple flags2.0—0.0$0Deducted once at the combined weight, not once per flag.
Total removed332.1-$9,558No percentage leakage: churn is on a members-lost basis and the card-at-risk deduction already holds the failing stock. Rows are rounded to one decimal, so they sum to 332.2 against the 332.1 total.
$9,542 per month separates the MRR presented from the MRR a buyer collects — 8.5% of the claimed figure, or about $114,500 of annual membership revenue. The earnings effect is smaller: section 04 takes $18,414 off EBITDA, worth $106,433 at 5.78x (shown as a memo in section 07). The deduction schedule above prices each removed member at the base ARPM of $28.78, which gives $9,558. The headline gap compares claimed MRR with collectible MRR directly, which gives $9,542. The difference is $16 a month, or 0.2%.

The top-down and calibrated demand figures differ by -36.7% in the 3-mile ring. That is outside the ±25% tolerance and says the 13-washes-per-vehicle assumption is too generous for this trade area. The engine is running on the calibrated basis, so the valuation is unaffected — but the gap should be closed before the ring is used to size a greenfield alternative.

Risk score components

ComponentReadingScoreWeightContributionBasis
Competitor density, 3 mi4.0048.022.0%10.6The first competitor within a mile has minimal impact; the third creates a documented cliff near one-third of activity (MMCG 6/2026).
Competitor density, 5 mi7.0042.010.0%4.2Wider ring density. Optimal submarkets carry 3-10 moderate-quality competitors.
Modeled share, 3 mi31.0823.818.0%4.3Absolute modeled share of the ring. Scored on a half-life curve: 15% share scores 50, and every further 15 points of share halves the risk. A smooth curve is used deliberately — a linear score against an equal split of the ring pins at zero for any site above parity, which leaves the component unable to register anything at all across the normal operating range.
Vehicles per tunnel, 3 mi9,22639.820.0%8.0Saturation floor of 6,942 vehicles per express tunnel, derived from 250 cars/day ideal volume over 361 operating days at 13 washes per vehicle a year. At the floor the component scores 50; each further multiple halves it, and thinner coverage pushes it up.

The single-site OpCo+PropCo band is 5.00x–7.00x (strong 7-8x, distressed 3-4x), stated on a fee-simple basis — EBITDA before any rent charge, real estate included — and applied exactly that way: enterprise value is EBITDA × multiple with no separate real-estate addition. The operating and real-estate figures above are a split of that one number. A quality score of 58.3 positions the multiple at 58% of the band, then 0.39 turns come off for the current competitive position (score 38.6); the pipeline is charged separately in the price bridge, so no competitor is priced twice. The seller note carries 7.00%. It is modeled on full standby, which is what SBA 7(a) requires before a seller note counts toward the equity injection (SOP 50 10 8, effective June 2025 — the note may cover at most half of the 10% injection, so cash must be at least 5%): no payments for the life of the SBA loan (it is repaid at exit in year 7), interest accruing, and the note excluded from the lender's coverage test. The accrued interest of $212,024 is paid at exit, taking the payoff to $562,024 against $350,000 of principal. That cost comes out of the equity proceeds and is the difference between an equity IRR that looks like a free $350,000 and one that is honestly priced.

EBITDA falls from $721,934 in year one to a trough of $513,029 in year three, then recovers to $644,045 by exit. That is the competitive pipeline working through the model: cars fall 7.7% a year in years 1 to 3 (118,000 to 92,687, or 21.5% in total) as the pipeline arrives, against an expected relative share loss of 26.20% in section 03, while operating expense grows about 3.5% a year and the model assumes price growth of 2.5% and cost inflation of 3.2%. Category demand growth is close to exhausted — professional wash adoption sits at 79% of US drivers against a practical ceiling MMCG puts near the low 80s — so the model assumes only modest growth (1.0% a year in cars, 2.0% in members, 2.5% in price), not a market that grows into the problem.

The plan takes normalized EBITDA from $798,486 to $1,062,238 and value from $4,615,249 to $6,139,736, for $154,000 of capital. None of it is priced into the supportable price in section 07 — this is what a buyer earns, not what a seller should be paid for. The voluntary-churn target of 2.4% and the 45% card-failure recovery together imply total churn of about 4.1% a month, below the 5-6% best-in-class band cited in this report. Paying for your own improvement plan is a common way a disciplined underwrite turns into an overpayment. The levers also overlap: more members lift the conversion bracket and enlarge the card-failure base, so they do not add cleanly. Several initiatives add revenue, so a true pro forma margin would be lower than the 61.5% ratio shown against today's revenue. That ratio sits above the 35–50% store-level benchmark, so treat the plan as an upper bound until each lever is tested.

Assumptions and sources

Every benchmark the report leans on, with its source and confidence grade.

Every benchmark in this report names its source. Where we found no credible published figure, the report says so rather than filling in a plausible number. Figures marked “our calculation” are derived by Wise Wash Partners from the cited primary source. Four gaps matter here and are flagged wherever they are used: we found no published car wash ground-lease cap rate, no published blended revenue per car, no published member wash frequency, and the trade-area saturation floor has an ambiguous denominator in its source.

Special situations

A clear path forward for car wash assets under pressure.

Wise Wash Partners steps in when a car wash loan defaults, a site loses members or an operator leaves. We assess the asset, keep it running and carry out a plan to stabilize it, working alongside the lender, owner and their advisors.

Discuss a challenged asset
Situations we handle

Six ways a car wash ends up on a lender’s watch list.

Loans in default
Payment or covenant defaults where the lender needs an operator’s view of the collateral.
Declining performance
Sites losing members, volume or margin faster than the market around them.
Operator departures
An owner or management team that has stepped away, leaving a site without leadership.
Receiverships
Court-appointed or private receiverships that need a car wash operator in place.
Portfolio pressure
Platforms with sites that are weighing on the whole portfolio.
Hard deadlines
A maturity, refinance or sale that needs a verified operating record on a short timeline.
The path forward

Assess, agree, carry it through.

Assess the asset

A condition, value and going-concern review of the site, with the membership base, equipment and financial position verified rather than assumed.

Agree the plan

Priorities, responsibilities, reporting and capital needs set with the lender, owner and their advisors, with verified projections for forbearance or workout discussions.

Carry it through

Interim management that keeps the site open, staffed and serving its members, alone or alongside a receiver, then stabilization and a verified record for a refinance, recapitalization or sale.

Alongside your team

We work within the lender’s or owner’s process, alongside their advisors, and report against the plan every month until the situation is resolved.

Operators, not observers

Our operating leadership has run car wash platforms of more than one hundred locations, and every assessment runs on our analytics platform.

Leadership

Capital markets, real estate and car wash operations, assessed together.

Wise Wash Partners pairs capital markets and real estate experience with senior car wash operating experience, so the capital decision and the operating reality are judged at the same table.

Frank Harris

Operations and underwriting

Frank has held four roles across the car wash industry. He built and ran his own flex-model wash to a premium average ticket, led operations as executive vice president for a national express brand across more than one hundred locations in multiple states, and as senior vice president of operations built a Southeast platform from the ground up.

Earlier, as a regional manager for a car wash chemical supplier, he worked the vendor side of the industry. He designed and built the firm’s analytics platform.

Ted Stone

Capital markets and real estate

Ted grew up in his family’s development business; the Stones began building residential subdivisions and homes in 1955. He studied commercial real estate, finance and development economics at Southern Methodist University before entering the industry full time.

Across several market cycles he has acquired, developed or capitalized more than five million square feet of commercial space and 4,000 acres of land, from raw land and entitlements through vertical development and long-term capitalization.

Jed Rollins

Investment and financial structuring

Jed’s experience centers on commercial real estate and spans investment, financial structuring and project execution. He has worked on complex projects collectively valued at more than $2 billion, with direct responsibility for structuring large-scale public-private partnerships and municipal financing arrangements.

Earlier, he founded an education-technology company and an entrepreneurial incubator, with responsibilities spanning business development, finance and day-to-day operations.
